coreTruths.title: Professionalism is a social contract, not a checklist of rules
coreTruths.broaderContext: Society grants dentists autonomy and self-regulation in exchange for placing patient welfare first. This contract shapes consent, advocacy, complaints, and every clinical decision.
coreTruths.body:
## Trust is the currency, and it has to be earned individually and collectively

The profession is granted autonomy, self-regulation, and a monopoly over its knowledge base in return for placing patient interests above its own and policing its own standards [1]. That trust is the only thing that makes the role workable, and it depends on individual integrity backed by collective regulation [2].

## Patient welfare comes first, and that creates real friction

A professional serves the patient's interests, not their wants. Politicians and even patients themselves are not always right [3]. Patients are entitled to ignore advice and seek care elsewhere, but they are not entitled to demand a treatment the clinician genuinely believes is not in their best interest [4].

## Autonomy and altruism are the two anchors

The principles boil down to primacy of patient welfare, patient autonomy through informed decisions, and fair allocation of resources [5]. Honesty about errors, confidentiality, no misuse of the relationship for personal gain, and disclosure of conflicts of interest sit underneath [6]. None of this is optional or sentimental, it is what holds the contract together.

## In the UK the GDC frames this as nine concrete duties

The Standards for the Dental Team operationalise the contract: put patients first, communicate effectively, get valid consent, protect their information, run a clear complaints procedure, work well with colleagues, stay within and develop your competence, raise concerns when patients are at risk, and behave in a way that maintains confidence in the profession [7].

citations.quote: Its members are governed by codes of ethics and profess a commitment to competence, integrity and morality, altruism, and to the promotion of the public good within their domain. These commitments form the basis of a social contract between the profession and society, which in return grants the profession a monopoly over the use of its knowledge base, the right to considerable autonomy in practice and the privilege of self-regulation. Professions and their members are accountable to those served and to society.

Individual and collective professional self-regulation lies at the heart of the concept of medical and dental professionalism. That is based on the precept that society trusts us with certain privileges by virtue of the job (in all its aspects) that we do and we maintain that trust by individual high standards of behaviour and collective regulation and remediation or censure of those who fail to live up to those standards.

The patient, individually or as a community, is not the customer who is always right. Politicians elected or unelected do not always have the best interests of the population at heart. In situations where we as professionals see this to be the case we are obliged to speak out.

Equally, a desperate avoidance of the appearance of being paternalistic in the name of political correctness becomes counterproductive if we fail to advise patients what we feel is in their best interests. They are entitled to ignore that advice (providing they are competent to do so) and go elsewhere but they are not entitled to demand that we provide a treatment we genuinely believe is not in their best interest.

Primacy of patient welfare. We serve the interests of our patient(s). Patient autonomy. We must empower patients to make informed decisions about their treatment. Social justice. Discrimination has no place in healthcare. Resources should be fairly allocated.
Probity with patients. Avoidance of any misuse of the relationship between professional and patient—for sexual, financial, or any personal advantage.

Put patients’ interests first, acting to protect them. Communicate effectively with patients. Obtain valid consent. Maintain and protect patients’ information. Have a clear and effective complaints procedure. Work with colleagues in a way that is in patients’ best interests. Maintain, develop, and work within your professional knowledge and skills. Raise concerns if patients are at risk. Make sure your personal behaviour maintains patients’ confidence in you and the dental profession.

coreTruths.title: Serious harm comes from system failure, not from one bad individual
coreTruths.broaderContext: Humans make mistakes. Disasters happen only when several latent failures line up. Treating error as systemic, not personal, is what actually reduces patient harm.
coreTruths.body:
## Mistakes are inevitable; harm is preventable

Everyone makes mistakes, that part is fixed [1]. What is variable is whether one mistake reaches the patient. Things go disastrously wrong only when several non-malicious errors compound, which is why the right unit of analysis is the system, not the individual [2].

## Swiss cheese: harm needs every defence to fail at once

The model is a stack of slices each with holes in different places. The error only reaches the patient if every hole lines up. A wrong drug might be prescribed, but the pharmacist catches it, or the patient knows their own allergy [3]. Designing redundancy into the patient journey is what blocks the straw from going through.

## Blame culture is the wrong tool

Finding someone to punish is the oldest reflex and the least useful one [4]. Reporting systems work when they are trusted, anonymised, and feed back something useful. They fail when an outside body imposes them, builds league tables, and gives no real feedback in return [5]. Critical event analysis only helps if the resulting changes actually reach the people doing the work [6].

## Stress narrows situational awareness, which is when errors slip through

Situational awareness is the bandwidth to track multiple things in the immediate environment. Stress collapses it and effectively blinkers the operator [7]. Watch for red flags, signs of an error in progress like an unexpected change to the operating list, and treat them as a cue to slow down [8].

## When the boss is wrong, escalate in graded steps

PACE gives a junior a way to challenge a senior without a stand-up row: probe, assert, confront, emergency [9]. Probe is a face-saving question. Assert raises the ante. Confront is point-of-no-return. Emergency is physical intervention to stop harm reaching the patient [10]. Knowing the script lowers the threshold to actually use it.

citations.quote: We all make mistakes, this is inevitable and inescapable. What is important is that the potential for serious harm coming from those mistakes is minimized and that we and others learn from those mistakes.

The recognition that humans make mistakes (that are usually non-malicious) but that things go disastrously wrong only when these mistakes are compounded, led to an approach where the system was analysed for failure rather than an individual being blamed.

For something to go seriously wrong (e.g. a patient dies from taking the wrongly prescribed drug), multiple failings have to happen. Think of trying to thread a straw through multiple layers of Swiss cheese. It will only pass through if all the holes, which are in different places on each slice, line up. One slice out of place and it won’t pass (i.e. the error won’t happen). In the patient analogy, the wrong drug might be prescribed, but the dispensing pharmacist might recognize this, or the patient might realize they were allergic to it.

A longstanding tradition of managing when things go wrong is to find out who is to blame and punish them. That’s it. It is astonishing that it has taken so long to accept that this is not the most useful way of going about things.

These have been successful where the system is trusted, usually anonymized, and reliable feedback is given. They have largely failed where a system has been imposed by an outside body which is not trusted (government or corporate body), league tables devised, and feedback has been minimal or useless.

This is supposed to happen after ‘clinical incident’ reporting, the idea being that the areas of system failure are identified and measures put in place to prevent failure at that point in the future. Obviously, this requires feedback and resource for change going to the people and places affected.

This is our capacity to be aware of multiple aspects of our immediate environment. A simple example would be driving behind a car which is travelling slower than you in the inside lane of a three-lane motorway at the point of a junction which has another car travelling at the same speed coming on the motorway. The calculation you make to position yourself safely without losing speed is your situational awareness. Stress massively reduces this and effectively blinkers you to potentially important outside influences.

This is the term given to the signs and symptoms of an error in progress. Recognition of a ‘red flag’, e.g. a change in the order of an operating list, should make everyone more aware of the potential for an error to occur.
If you are working in a hierarchy, how do you tell the boss he or she is doing something wrong? One excellent technique is the PACE approach.
‘Stop. I am not going to let this happen.’ An extreme situation where you intervene (possibly even physically) to prevent harm to a patient.

coreTruths.title: Effective clinical communication is structured, not improvised charm
coreTruths.broaderContext: Listening, preparation, and consistency carry more weight than verbal fluency. Structured communication earns consent, defuses bad news, and prevents the most common complaints.
coreTruths.body:
## Two ears, one mouth, and they are rarely used in those proportions

Active listening is the harder skill and the more rewarding one [1]. Don't interrupt unless essential, and if interruption was unavoidable, give the person a way back to the point they were making [2].

## Time, preparation, and the right words

Breaking news, especially bad news, takes time the clinician has to allocate, allow, and stick to [3]. Prepare what to say and how to say it before the conversation starts [4]. Words carry weight: "sorry" can land as an admission of guilt or as sincere empathy depending on timing, intonation, and body language [5]. Honesty does not mean dumping every detail, that just clears the clinician's conscience while harming the patient [6].

## After bad news, ask how they feel

After delivering bad news, the most useful question is often "How do you feel about that?" The range of responses is wider than expected and giving people room to say it is what makes the consultation real [7]. People will have questions but may need time to refocus, so suggest they write them down for next time [7].

## Consistency across the team prevents most complaints

Few things disorientate a patient more than being told different things by different people about the same problem [8]. Before launching into a detailed explanation, ask the patient what they have already been told and what they understood. If a previous account was wrong, correct it openly and explain how the misunderstanding happened [8].

## Empathy with boundaries

Empathy and compassion belong in every consultation, but the clinician is not a limitless source and not an emotional punchbag. Boundaries are what prevent burnout, and burnout is what eventually erodes everything else [9].

## Build rapport deliberately, not by accident

Matching body language, eye contact, tone of voice, and active listening are how rapport is built in real time. Seek first to understand, then to be understood [10]. Begin every meaningful interaction with a clear sense of the outcome wanted, frameworks like SMART help when the goal needs to be specific, measurable, achievable, realistic, and time-bound [11].

citations.quote: We have two ears and one mouth, but they are rarely used in those proportions.

This is hard to do but hugely rewarding. Try to cultivate an active listening style; don’t interrupt unless it is essential and if you do, always give the opportunity to come back to a point that may be vital to them at some time in the future.
Time is needed to learn these skills, to use them in imparting news (especially bad news) to people, and to allow people to absorb that news. Allocate it, allow it, and stick to it.
When communicating, it is helpful to be sure of the information you are imparting and that you want to impart it. Prepare what you want or have to say as well as how you will say it.
Saying ‘sorry’ can be taken as an admission of guilt or as a sincere form of empathy. Timing, intonation, and body language influence how the same word is understood by the person hearing it.
Honesty is best but does not mean burdening someone with extraneous detail which clears your conscience but unnecessarily harms someone else.

People will have questions but may need time to refocus to ask them—suggest they write them down for next time. They will also have a legitimate need to have some answered—if you can, do so, but don’t be afraid to admit you don’t know. If you can’t, but know someone who can, then that is a fair response. Equally you may ask questions; the most useful after breaking bad news, perhaps surprisingly, is ‘How do you feel about that?’ The number of different responses will astonish you and it is of huge importance to let people express themselves at this point.

Few things are more disorientating than being told different things by different people about the same subject, especially if that subject is your personal health or that of a loved one. Be sure of what has been said before—ask the person you are talking to as it is what they remember or understand that is important to the conversation. Try to ensure all team members do this before launching into some detailed explanation which may be at odds with what has gone before. If previous information is incorrect it must be corrected but include an explanation of how that ‘misunderstanding’ arose.

These are important components of communication but this does not mean you are a limitless source nor does it mean you are an emotional punchbag for upset individuals. Having boundaries in your role as a professional communicator is essential to prevent burn out.

When communicating with others, build rapport—this can be done through matching body language, eye contact, tone of voice (pace and leading), and active listening. Understand the situation from the other person’s perspective, ‘Seek first to understand, then to be understood’.
SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, and defined Time frame).

coreTruths.title: People differ in personality and learning style, and ignoring that breeds stress and resistance
coreTruths.broaderContext: No one personality type is best, but forcing someone to operate outside theirs creates stress, error, and failed change. Recognising difference is a clinical and managerial skill.
coreTruths.body:
## No personality type is better, but each suits different roles

No single personality type is superior, the point is that certain types fit certain roles and certain ways of learning. Forcing someone to act outside their type causes real stress [1]. Frameworks like Myers-Briggs sort preferences along introversion/extraversion, sensing/intuiting, thinking/feeling, and judging/perceiving, going through the process is itself useful for self-insight [2].

## Learning has stages, and people prefer different ones

Learning has four stages: reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, active experimentation, and concrete experience. Most people prefer one stage and feel uncomfortable when forced into another [3]. Teaching that ignores this lands badly, even if the content is right.

## Imposed change usually fails; ownership is what makes it stick

Most imposed change fails because professionals' inertia is enormous when consultation is facile and the evidence base is missing [4]. Hearts-and-minds approaches outperform punitive ones for educated professionals [5]. Treating organisations as machines whose components can be told what to do is a recipe for failed change, treating them as evolving ecosystems steered by simple rules works better [6].

## Emotional intelligence is the lever

For individuals to live with change they need emotional intelligence: recognising their own feelings and others', motivating themselves, and managing emotions in relationships [7]. Working out what motivates the person is how they come to feel they own the change, which is the single biggest predictor of whether the change actually holds [7].

## Leadership is enabling, not commanding

Real leadership is keeping things together and putting the right people in the right place at the right time, not always being right or always in front [8]. A good leader becomes a follower temporarily when someone else has the better skill set for the moment [8].

citations.quote: While no human being is completely stereotyped into a category with regard to both personality and learning preferences, most of us show tendencies towards various behaviour types. It is important to realize that no one type is better than another but that certain types are more suited to certain roles in life and certain ways of learning new information, skills, or behaviours and that being forced to act outside that type can lead to significant stress.

This is a gross simplification of the process but gives you an idea of how people can differ, no one ‘type’ (indicated by the letters allocated to the different sections) is better than another but certain types cope better in certain situations, jobs, roles, and in interpersonal relationships. Just going through the process aids in personal insight and reflective capability.

Just as there are four distinct personality traits which flow into each other so there are equivalent learning types. These also match the stages of learning and reflection and development of what has already been learned. The distinction between people is that they tend to prefer one stage more than another and can feel uncomfortable or even stressed if forced into an area they are less comfortable in.

The intense resentment felt by most professionals towards change has come about by imposed change, with no or facile consultation, no evidence base, and no internal motivation for that change. The fact that most of these imposed changes fail, often due to the incredible power of healthcare professionals’ inertia even in the absence of tacit opposition, is a lesson that those who would impose change continually fail to learn.

There are two which are not mutually exclusive but tend to have different emphasis: changing attitudes in the relevant individuals and hoping that behavioural change will follow (‘hearts and minds’) and a more punitive approach emphasizing the legal and business reasons for change. While the latter has become increasingly popular it is unsurprisingly less effective with highly motivated and educated healthcare professionals.

There is an unfortunate tendency for many trying to implement change to stick with conventional management theory which looks on organizations as machines with staff as components of that machine. This leads to the folly that a detailed plan for change can be worked out in advance (often by outsiders), people are told what to do and will both do it and do it consistently, and that this process will be automatically replicable from one area to another. A much more useful concept is that organizations are complex evolving ecosystems functioning on a series of interdependent nested systems.

For individuals to function effectively with change they need to develop emotional intelligence: ‘the capacity for recognizing our own feelings and those of others, for motivating ourselves and for managing emotions well in ourselves and in our relationships’. Discovering what motivates ourselves and others is the key technique in ensuring people feel they ‘own’ the change and the change process, the key aspect of successful change management.

True leadership is about keeping things together, using the right people in the right place at the right time to achieve an agreed goal. Followership is acknowledging this and the leader who gives way (and becomes a ‘follower’ temporarily) to allow someone with a more appropriate skill set to lead is enabling that to happen.
